Affiliation:: Department of Mathematics, University of Oklahoma
Techniques Used: Definitions of maximal, almost maximal, and infinitesimal maximal symmetry
Analysis of Der(s) (derivations of a Lie algebra)
Application Areas: Proving or addressing the Alekseevskii Conjecture
Classification and structural understanding of homogeneous Einstein spaces
Understanding the stability of Einstein metrics under the Ricci flow
Determining the uniqueness of Ricci solitons on solvable Lie groups
Structural theory and classification of semi-simple Lie algebras
Geometric representation theory (finding faithful representations that are also isometric embeddings)
Relating complex geometric objects (Einstein solvmanifolds) to classical ones (symmetric spaces)
Key Research Thinking Patterns: Reductionism: Solves complex problems by first reducing them to simpler, more structured cases (e.g. reducing problems on general solvable Lie groups to the completely solvable case or reducing properties of a solvable group to its nilradical)

Conceptual Generalization: Extends existing concepts to broaden their applicability and solve related problems (e.g. generalizing "maximal symmetry" to "infinitesimal maximal symmetry" to successfully analyze Ricci solitons).

Interdisciplinary Tool Application: Applies techniques from one mathematical field to solve problems in another (e.g., using Geometric Invariant Theory to prove results about Einstein solvmanifolds or using Einstein solvmanifold geometry to determine properties of Lie algebras).

Constructive Decomposition: Proves existence by constructively building a solution based on a deep structural decomposition of the object (e.g. using eigenspace and Iwasawa decompositions to build isometric embeddings or reconstruct a semi-simple Lie algebra).
Summary Description: Michael R. Jablonski is a leading researcher in Differential Geometry and Lie Theory, applying advanced structural and geometric techniques to Riemannian Geometry, Lie Algebras, and Representation Theory. His work features foundational contributions, including proving Einstein solvmanifolds have maximal symmetry , using "infinitesimal maximal symmetry" to show Ricci solitons have maximal isometry algebras , and isometrically embedding Einstein and Ricci soliton solvmanifolds into symmetric spaces. His research connects geometric properties (like symmetry and curvature) to algebraic structure , reduces complex problems to simpler, structured cases , and applies tools like Geometric Invariant Theory to provide foundational insights into homogeneous spaces.
